title: Some Thoughts on Whole-Soul Professional Development
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart critiques professional development designed solely for the intellect, arguing that PD aimed only at cognitive understanding fails to produce lasting change because educators are whole persons with interrelated intellectual, emotional, physical, and social dimensions. He introduces the four-part soul model as a framework for designing PD that touches the whole person, and illustrates each dimension with concrete facilitator moves: using stories and anecdotes for intellectual retention, drawing on hope and nostalgia for emotional engagement, making group members' contributions visible for social deepening, and showing what strategies look like in practice for physical grounding. Stuart distinguishes intentional emotional engagement from manipulative emotional conjuring, defending the former as a legitimate facilitation tool. The article argues that whole-soul PD is not an aspirational ideal but a practical and achievable framework. Sessions designed this way are more likely to produce participants who leave both feeling encouraged and being equipped — the dual standard most schools seek.
points: PD aimed only at the intellect fails because understanding alone does not produce lasting change; the emotional, physical, and social dimensions of the whole person must also be engaged.
The most common PD failure is the HOW gap: telling people to think differently is not the same as showing them how to begin doing so in the actualities of daily life.
Stories, anecdotes, and cross-discipline examples serve intellectual memory in PD — they are not decorative but functionally necessary for lasting uptake of new ideas.

Facilitators can legitimately intend to draw out feelings — particularly hope and nostalgia — without being manipulative, because these reconnect teachers to the core motivation that brought them to education.
Going big on peer-contributed examples during sessions is the key social move: it uses the group to grow the group and signals that practitioner knowledge has real value in the PD space.
quotes: it was all aimed at my head! The presenter's working theory seemed to be that if I'd just think and understand correctly, then all would be well for me, and my life would be better ever after.

Telling me that I should start thinking a new way isn't the same thing as showing me HOW to start thinking that way in the actualities of my everyday life. For understandings to change us, they have to work their way in deep.
Human beings aren't brains on sticks — we're souls. We've got these interrelated parts, each of which must be engaged, in order for change to truly last.

it drives me crazy when I attend PD in which I feel like the speaker is trying to conjure up feelings in the audience. But over time, I've learned that it's not inherently wrong to intend to draw out certain feelings in folks when you're leading PD. My favorite feelings to draw on are hope and nostalgia.

I work to draw people back to the central drive that made them an educator to begin with. I throw fuel on the fire of that hope by emphatically and repetitively making the case that the work of education is fundamentally good and worthy.

what I'm calling whole-soul PD isn't some pie-in-the-sky idea but is instead a very practical, createable kind of thing. It's a robust framework for increasing the likelihood that folks will leave today's session feeling encouraged and being equipped, which is what so many of my client schools are after when they reach out to me.
